title: Chapter 10: Guardrails, Safety, and Hallucination Control
content:
Chapter 10: Guardrails, Safety, and Hallucination Control

Opening Hook: A Good AI Demo Can Still Fail in Real Life

An AI demo can look amazing.

It can answer quickly. It can sound confident. It can summarize documents. It can use tools. It can remember context. It can draft proposals. It can produce polished reports.

Then a real user asks:

Can you delete all old client files?

or:

Can you guarantee this contract is legally safe?

or:

Here is my API key. Remember it for later.

or:

Send this email to the client without showing me first.

Suddenly, the app needs more than intelligence.

It needs boundaries.

Those boundaries are called guardrails.

Guardrails are rules, checks, validations, and review steps that help an AI application behave more safely and reliably.

This chapter is not about making your AI app perfect.

No guardrail system is perfect.

This chapter is about making your AI app more responsible, more predictable, and more professional.

In this chapter, you will build a guarded assistant that checks user input, detects risky requests, validates model output, and triggers human review when needed.

This is one of the chapters that separates a toy AI demo from a serious AI application.

What You Will Learn

By the end of this chapter, you will understand:

  • Why AI agents fail
  • What hallucinations are
  • What guardrails are
  • How to check user input before calling the model
  • How to detect risky requests
  • How to reject or route unsafe requests
  • How to validate AI output
  • How to add human review triggers
  • How to reduce hallucinations with prompt rules
  • How to design safer AI workflows
  • How to test guardrail logic without making API calls
  • How guardrails improve portfolio and client-ready AI projects

Why This Chapter Matters

In earlier chapters, you built powerful capabilities:

  • RAG for documents
  • Semantic search
  • Tool calling
  • Memory
  • Workflow automation
  • Multi-agent workflows

Each capability adds value.

Each capability also adds risk.

A RAG app can retrieve the wrong chunk. A tool-using agent can call the wrong function. A memory assistant can store sensitive information. A workflow agent can draft misleading client messages. A research workflow can create unsupported claims.

The more capable your AI agent becomes, the more carefully you need to design its boundaries.

A professional AI builder asks:

What could go wrong?

Then builds checks around those failure points.

That is what guardrails are for.

10.1 What Are Guardrails?

Guardrails are protective checks around an AI application.

They can happen before the model call, after the model call, or before an action is taken.

A basic guardrail system looks like this:

User input
↓
Input guardrail
↓
AI model or agent
↓
Output validation
↓
Human review check
↓
Final response

Guardrails can include:

  • Blocking empty or extremely long input
  • Detecting secrets such as API keys
  • Detecting risky actions
  • Refusing unsafe requests
  • Requiring human review
  • Validating JSON output
  • Checking for unsupported claims
  • Requiring source citations
  • Preventing dangerous tool calls
  • Adding disclaimers for sensitive domains
  • Logging risky events

Guardrails do not make an app flawless.

They reduce predictable risks.

10.2 What Is a Hallucination?

A hallucination is an AI output that sounds confident but is unsupported, misleading, or false.

Example:

The document says refunds are available for 90 days.

But the document never said that.

Or:

According to a 2025 study, 89% of businesses use this tool.

But no study was provided.

Hallucinations are dangerous because AI-generated text can sound polished and authoritative.

A hallucination can happen when:

  • The model does not have enough context
  • The prompt asks for information not provided
  • Retrieval returns the wrong chunks
  • The user asks for current facts without a source
  • The model is asked to guess
  • The workflow lacks validation
  • The system rewards fluency instead of accuracy

Your goal is not to eliminate hallucinations completely.

Your goal is to design your app so it is less likely to hallucinate and more likely to admit uncertainty.

10.3 Common AI Agent Failure Modes

AI agents can fail in many ways.

Failure TypeExamplePrevention
HallucinationInvents factsUse RAG, source rules, uncertainty rules
Bad retrievalRetrieves wrong document chunkInspect retrieved context
Unsafe tool useCalls risky functionUse tool allowlists
Memory misuseStores secretsAdd memory safety checks
Over-automationSends email without reviewAdd human approval
Bad JSONReturns invalid structureValidate output
OverconfidenceGives legal or medical certaintyAdd sensitive-domain guardrails
Privacy leakReveals stored memoryLimit memory usage
Cost spikeToo many agent loopsAdd call limits
Poor UXBlocks too muchUse clear review messages

Guardrails are not one feature.

They are a design mindset.

10.4 Three Types of Guardrails

1. Input Guardrails

Input guardrails check the user’s message before it reaches the model.

Examples:

Is the input empty?
Is the input too long?
Does it contain an API key?
Is the user asking for a destructive action?
Is the user asking for sensitive professional advice?

2. Output Guardrails

Output guardrails check the model’s response before showing it to the user.

Examples:

Is the output empty?
Is the output too long?
Does it include prohibited claims?
Does it follow the required format?
Does it need human review?

3. Action Guardrails

Action guardrails check before the app does something in the real world.

Examples:

Before sending an email, ask for approval.
Before deleting a file, ask for approval.
Before updating a database, ask for approval.
Before calling a paid API many times, confirm.

Action guardrails are especially important for tool-using agents.

10.5 The Human-in-the-Loop Pattern

A human-in-the-loop system keeps a person involved in important decisions.

This does not make the AI weaker.

It makes the system safer.

Use human approval before:

  • Sending emails
  • Making purchases
  • Deleting files
  • Updating client records
  • Giving legal conclusions
  • Giving medical conclusions
  • Giving financial conclusions
  • Sharing private data
  • Storing sensitive memory
  • Taking irreversible actions

The best beginner rule is:

AI drafts. Human approves. System acts only after approval.

You used this rule in Chapter 8.

In this chapter, you will implement it more directly.

10.6 Project: Guarded AI Assistant

What This Project Does

This project builds a guarded assistant that can summarize or answer user-provided text while applying guardrails.

It will:

  1. Check user input
  2. Detect risky categories
  3. Block unsafe requests
  4. Add human review warnings
  5. Call the LLM only when appropriate
  6. Validate the output
  7. Trigger review if the response is risky
  8. Show a clear final answer

Who This Helps

This project helps:

  • Developers building safer AI apps
  • Freelancers creating client-ready AI tools
  • Students improving portfolio projects
  • Teams adding validation to prototypes
  • Anyone building RAG, tools, memory, or workflow agents

What You Will Build

pip install -r requirements.txt

Create llm_client.py:

"""
Chapter 10: Reusable LLM Client
"""

import os from dataclasses import dataclass, field from dotenv import load_dotenv from openai import OpenAI

load_dotenv()

def get_env_float(name: str, default: float) -> float:

"""Read a float from environment variables safely."""

raw_value = os.getenv(name)

if raw_value is None:
return default

try:

return float(raw_value)

except ValueError:
return default

@dataclass

class LLMConfig:

"""Configuration for the LLM client."""

model: str = field(
 default_factory=lambda: os.getenv("OPENAI_MODEL", "gpt-4.1-mini")
 )
 temperature: float = field(
 default_factory=lambda: get_env_float("OPENAI_TEMPERATURE", 0.2)
 )

class LLMClient:

"""Small reusable client for sending prompts to an LLM."""

def __init__(self, config: LLMConfig | None = None):
 self.config = config or LLMConfig()
 api_key = os.getenv("OPENAI_API_KEY")

if not api_key:
raise ValueError(
"OPENAI_API_KEY is missing. Add it to your .env file."
)

self.client = OpenAI(api_key=api_key)

def complete(self, system: str, user: str) -> str:
"""Send a request to the model and return text output."""

if not system.strip():
 raise ValueError("System instruction cannot be empty.")
if not user.strip():
 raise ValueError("User request cannot be empty.")

model_input = f"""
System instruction:

{system.strip()}

User request:

{user.strip()}

"""

response = self.client.responses.create(
model=self.config.model,
input=model_input,
temperature=self.config.temperature,
)

return response.output_text

10.10 File: guardrails.py

Create guardrails.py:

"""
Input guardrails for the Chapter 10 guarded assistant.

These checks are beginner-friendly examples. They reduce predictable risks,
but they are not a complete safety system.
"""

import re from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass

class RiskAssessment:

"""Result of an input or output risk check."""

allowed: bool
needs_human_review: bool
risk_level: str
reason: str
categories: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

DESTRUCTIVE_ACTION_KEYWORDS = [
"delete all",
"remove all",
"wipe",
"erase",
"drop database",
"shutdown",
"format disk",
]

SENSITIVE_ADVICE_KEYWORDS = [
"legal advice",
"medical diagnosis",
"diagnose me",
"investment advice",
"tax advice",
"is this contract safe",
"should i invest",
]

EXTERNAL_ACTION_KEYWORDS = [
"send email",
"send this",
"submit",
"purchase",
"buy this",
"transfer money",
"make payment",
"post this",
]

SECRET_KEYWORDS = [
"api key",
"password",
"private key",
"secret key",
"access token",
"bearer token",
]

def contains_any(text: str, keywords: list[str]) -> bool:

"""Return True if text contains any keyword."""

lowered = text.lower()

return any(keyword in lowered for keyword in keywords)

def looks_like_secret(text: str) -> bool:

"""
Detect text that may contain secrets.

This is a basic heuristic, not a complete secret scanner.
"""

lowered = text.lower()

if contains_any(lowered, SECRET_KEYWORDS):
return True

secret_patterns = [
r"sk-[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}",
r"api[_-]?key\s*[:=]\s*[A-Za-z0-9_\-]{10,}",
r"password\s*[:=]\s*\S+",
r"token\s*[:=]\s*[A-Za-z0-9_\-\.]{10,}",
]

return any(re.search(pattern, text, re.IGNORECASE) for pattern in secret_patterns)

def assess_input(text: str, max_chars: int = 6000) -> RiskAssessment:

"""
Assess user input before sending it to the model.
"""

cleaned = text.strip()

if not cleaned:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False,
needs_human_review=False,
risk_level="low",
reason="Input is empty.",
categories=["empty_input"],
)

if len(cleaned) > max_chars:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False,
needs_human_review=True,
risk_level="medium",
reason=f"Input is too long for this beginner demo. Limit: {max_chars} characters.",
categories=["too_long"],
)

categories = []

if looks_like_secret(cleaned):
categories.append("possible_secret")

if contains_any(cleaned, DESTRUCTIVE_ACTION_KEYWORDS):
categories.append("destructive_action")

if contains_any(cleaned, EXTERNAL_ACTION_KEYWORDS):
categories.append("external_action")

if contains_any(cleaned, SENSITIVE_ADVICE_KEYWORDS):
categories.append("sensitive_advice")

if "possible_secret" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False,
needs_human_review=True,
risk_level="high",
reason=(
"This input appears to contain sensitive information such as a secret, "
"password, token, or API key. Do not send secrets to the assistant."
),
categories=categories,
)

if "destructive_action" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=False,
needs_human_review=True,
risk_level="high",
reason=(
"This request appears to involve a destructive or irreversible action. "
"Human review is required, and this demo will not perform the action."
),
categories=categories,
)

if "external_action" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=True,
needs_human_review=True,
risk_level="medium",
reason=(
"This request appears to involve an external action. The assistant may draft, "
"but a human should approve before anything is sent, submitted, or purchased."
),
categories=categories,
)

if "sensitive_advice" in categories:

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=True,
needs_human_review=True,
risk_level="medium",
reason=(
"This request may involve sensitive professional advice. The assistant can provide "
"general information, but a qualified professional should review important decisions."
),
categories=categories,
)

return RiskAssessment(

allowed=True,
needs_human_review=False,
risk_level="low",
reason="No obvious risk detected.",
categories=[],
)

def format_risk_assessment(assessment: RiskAssessment) -> str:

"""Format risk assessment for display."""

categories = ", ".join(assessment.categories) if assessment.categories else "none"

return f"""
Risk level: {assessment.risk_level}
Allowed: {assessment.allowed}
Needs human review: {assessment.needs_human_review}
Categories: {categories}
Reason: {assessment.reason}
""".strip()

10.11 File: validators.py

Create validators.py:

"""
Output validation helpers for the Chapter 10 guarded assistant.
"""

from dataclasses import dataclass, field

@dataclass

class ValidationResult:

"""Result of output validation."""

passed: bool
needs_human_review: bool
reason: str
issues: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)

PROHIBITED_PHRASES = [
"i guarantee",
"100% accurate",
"no risk",
"definitely legal",
"definitely safe",
"you do not need a lawyer",
"you do not need a doctor",
"this is financial advice",
"this is legal advice",
"this is a medical diagnosis",
]

def contains_prohibited_phrase(text: str) -> list[str]:

"""Return prohibited phrases found in text."""

lowered = text.lower()

return [phrase for phrase in PROHIBITED_PHRASES if phrase in lowered]

def validate_output_text(

text: str,
 min_chars: int = 20,
 max_chars: int = 5000,
) -> ValidationResult:
 """
 Validate a model response before displaying it.
 """
cleaned = text.strip()
 issues = []

if not cleaned:

return ValidationResult(

passed=False,
needs_human_review=True,
reason="Output is empty.",
issues=["empty_output"],
)

if len(cleaned) < min_chars:
issues.append("too_short")

if len(cleaned) > max_chars:
issues.append("too_long")

prohibited = contains_prohibited_phrase(cleaned)

if prohibited:
issues.append("prohibited_phrase")

if issues:

return ValidationResult(

passed=False,
needs_human_review=True,
reason="Output failed validation checks.",
issues=issues,
)

return ValidationResult(

passed=True,
needs_human_review=False,
reason="Output passed validation.",
issues=[],
)

def validate_required_sections(text: str, required_sections: list[str]) -> ValidationResult:

"""
Check whether output contains required section labels.
"""

cleaned = text.lower()
 missing = []

for section in required_sections:
if section.lower() not in cleaned:
missing.append(section)

if missing:

return ValidationResult(

passed=False,
needs_human_review=True,
reason="Output is missing required sections.",
issues=[f"missing_section:{section}" for section in missing],
)

return ValidationResult(

passed=True,
needs_human_review=False,
reason="All required sections are present.",
issues=[],
)

def format_validation_result(result: ValidationResult) -> str:

"""Format validation result for display."""

issues = ", ".join(result.issues) if result.issues else "none"

return f"""
Validation passed: {result.passed}
Needs human review: {result.needs_human_review}
Issues: {issues}
Reason: {result.reason}
""".strip()

10.12 File: review.py

Create review.py:

"""
Human review checklist helpers for the Chapter 10 guarded assistant.
"""

from guardrails import RiskAssessment from validators import ValidationResult

def build_review_checklist(

input_assessment: RiskAssessment,
output_validation: ValidationResult | None = None,
) -> list[str]:
"""
Build a human review checklist based on risk and validation results.
"""

checklist = [
"Review the AI output before using it.",
"Check that the response does not invent facts.",
"Check that the response matches the user's actual request.",
"Check that no sensitive information is exposed.",
]

if input_assessment.needs_human_review:
checklist.append(
"Input risk was detected. Confirm the request is safe and appropriate."
)

if "sensitive_advice" in input_assessment.categories:
checklist.append(
"For legal, medical, financial, or tax topics, consult a qualified professional."
)

if "external_action" in input_assessment.categories:
checklist.append(
"Do not send, submit, post, purchase, or transfer anything without explicit human approval."
)

if "destructive_action" in input_assessment.categories:
checklist.append(
"Do not perform destructive or irreversible actions from this assistant."
)

if output_validation and output_validation.needs_human_review:
checklist.append(
"Output validation flagged issues. Review carefully before using the response."
)

if output_validation and output_validation.issues:
checklist.append(
f"Validation issues found: {', '.join(output_validation.issues)}"
)

return checklist

def format_review_checklist(checklist: list[str]) -> str:

"""Format review checklist as Markdown checkboxes."""

if not checklist:

return "- [ ] Review AI output before using it."

return "\n".join(f"- [ ] {item}" for item in checklist)

10.13 File: guarded_assistant.py

Create guarded_assistant.py:

"""
Guarded assistant logic for Chapter 10.
"""

from llm_client import LLMClient from guardrails import assess_input, format_risk_assessment from validators import validate_output_text, format_validation_result from review import build_review_checklist, format_review_checklist

GUARDED_SYSTEM_PROMPT = """
You are a careful AI assistant.

Your job is to help the user with summaries, explanations, and safe drafts.

Rules:
- Do not invent facts.
- Do not claim certainty when information is missing.
- Do not provide legal, medical, financial, or tax conclusions.
- For sensitive topics, provide general information and recommend qualified review.
- Do not claim that you performed external actions.
- Do not say you sent, deleted, purchased, submitted, or updated anything.
- If the user asks for a risky action, explain that human review is required.
- Keep the response clear and practical.
"""

def build_guarded_prompt(user_input: str, review_note: str = "") -> str:

"""
Build the prompt for the guarded assistant.
"""

return f"""
User input:

{user_input}

Risk/review note:

{review_note or "No special review note."}

Task:
Respond helpfully and safely.

If the user provided text to summarize, summarize it.
If the user asked a question, answer carefully.
If the user requested an external or risky action, do not claim it was done.
Instead, provide a draft or checklist for human review.
"""

def run_guarded_assistant(user_input: str) -> str:

"""
Run input guardrails, model call, output validation, and review handling.
"""

input_assessment = assess_input(user_input)

if not input_assessment.allowed:
checklist = build_review_checklist(input_assessment)

return f"""
Request blocked or requires manual handling.

{format_risk_assessment(input_assessment)}

Human Review Checklist:

{format_review_checklist(checklist)}

""".strip()

review_note = ""

if input_assessment.needs_human_review:
review_note = input_assessment.reason

client = LLMClient()
 prompt = build_guarded_prompt(
 user_input=user_input,
 review_note=review_note,
 )

response = client.complete(
system=GUARDED_SYSTEM_PROMPT,
user=prompt,
)

validation = validate_output_text(response)

if not validation.passed or input_assessment.needs_human_review:
checklist = build_review_checklist(
input_assessment=input_assessment,
output_validation=validation,
)

return f"""
Assistant Draft:

{response}

---

Review Information:

{format_risk_assessment(input_assessment)}

{format_validation_result(validation)}

Human Review Checklist:

{format_review_checklist(checklist)}

""".strip()

return response

"""

from guarded_assistant import run_guarded_assistant

def main() -> None:

"""Run the guarded assistant."""

## 10.19 How the Code Works
This project has four major layers.
### Layer 1: Input Guardrails
The assess_input() function checks the user request.

Very long input

The assistant blocks the request.
### Layer 2: Model Call
If the input is allowed, the assistant calls the model.
The system prompt includes safety rules such as:

This is important because the assistant should not pretend to perform actions.
### Layer 3: Output Validation
The validate_output_text() function checks the model’s response.
It looks for:
Empty output
Very short output
Very long output
Prohibited claims
Example prohibited phrases include:
I guarantee
100% accurate
definitely legal
no risk
These phrases are risky because they create false certainty.
### Layer 4: Human Review Checklist
If the input or output needs review, the app builds a checklist.
Example:
- [ ] Review the AI output before using it.
- [ ] Check that the response does not invent facts.
- [ ] Do not send, submit, post, purchase, or transfer anything without explicit human approval.
This keeps the human in control.

## 10.23 Guardrails for RAG Apps
In Chapter 4, you built a PDF RAG assistant.
RAG apps need guardrails too.
Common RAG guardrails include:
Answer only from retrieved context.
If the answer is missing, say it is not found.
Show source pages.
Do not invent citations.
Do not use outside knowledge unless allowed.
A RAG system should also test:
What happens when retrieval is wrong?
What happens when no chunks are retrieved?
What happens when the user asks for something not in the document?
What happens when the document contains sensitive information?
What happens when multiple chunks conflict?
A strong RAG app should not simply sound confident.
It should show where the answer came from.

## 10.24 Guardrails for Tool-Using Agents
In Chapter 6, you built a tool-using agent.
Tool-using agents need action guardrails.
Examples:
Only allow approved tools.
Validate tool inputs.
Reject unknown tools.
Require approval before external actions.
Log tool calls.
Use timeouts for API calls.
Avoid destructive tools.
The tool registry from Chapter 6 is itself a guardrail.
It prevents the model from inventing tools like:
delete_database
send_payment
run_shell_command
A tool-using agent should never be allowed to run arbitrary actions without control.

In Chapter 7, you built a memory assistant.
Memory systems need privacy guardrails.
Examples:
Do not store secrets.
Let users inspect memory.
Let users delete memory.
Save only user-approved facts.
Separate memory by user.
Avoid logging private memory.
A memory assistant should not silently remember everything.

In Chapter 8, you built a freelance automation agent.
Workflow automation needs human approval guardrails.
Examples:

Do not invent deadlines.

Add a review checklist.
Client-facing AI output should be treated as a draft.

## 10.27 Guardrails for Multi-Agent Workflows
In Chapter 9, you built a research workflow.
Multi-agent workflows need factual-risk guardrails.
Examples:
Do not invent statistics.
Do not invent citations.
Mark claims that need verification.
Save intermediate outputs.
Use reviewer agents.
Review final output before publication.
Multi-agent workflows can sound impressive, but they can also amplify errors.
If the researcher invents a claim, the writer may polish it, and the reviewer may miss it.
That is why the workflow should save intermediate steps.

## 10.28 Reducing Hallucinations
You cannot fully eliminate hallucinations, but you can reduce them.
Use these techniques.
### 1. Provide Context
Bad:
What does the policy say about refunds?
Better:
Using only the retrieved policy chunks below, answer the question.
### 2. Require Uncertainty
Add:
If the answer is not in the context, say you could not find it.
### 3. Show Sources
Use page numbers, document names, or source snippets.
### 4. Avoid Guessing Prompts
Bad:
Guess what the document means.
Better:
Summarize only what the document explicitly states.
### 5. Validate Output
Check for prohibited phrases, missing sections, and unsupported certainty.
### 6. Use Review Steps
For important output, add a reviewer agent or human review checklist.
### 7. Test Unanswerable Questions
Ask questions that should produce:
I could not find that in the document.
A RAG app that cannot say “not found” is not ready.

## 10.29 Security and Privacy Basics
AI app security is a broad topic, but beginner projects should follow these basics.
### Protect Secrets
Never hardcode API keys.
Never store secrets in memory.
Never publish .env files.
### Limit Tool Access
Do not give the model unrestricted access to files, databases, shell commands, or payment systems.
### Use Human Approval
Require approval before external or irreversible actions.
### Avoid Sensitive Logs
Do not log private data, secrets, or confidential client information.
### Separate Users
A real multi-user app needs separate user data storage.
### Use Least Privilege
Give each tool only the permissions it needs.
### Review Dependencies
Keep packages updated and review what they do before using them in production.

## 10.32 Common Mistakes
### Mistake 1: Adding Guardrails Too Late
Safety should not be an afterthought.
Design guardrails while designing the app.
### Mistake 2: Assuming RAG Prevents Hallucinations
RAG helps, but bad retrieval can still produce bad answers.
### Mistake 3: Letting Tools Run Without Approval
Tool-using agents need strict controls.
### Mistake 4: Storing Secrets in Memory
Memory should not store API keys, passwords, or private tokens.
### Mistake 5: Trusting Polished Output
Clear writing does not guarantee correctness.
### Mistake 6: Not Testing Bad Inputs
Test risky prompts on purpose.
### Mistake 7: Blocking Everything
A useful guardrail system should not reject every difficult request.
Sometimes the right response is:
I can draft this for human review.
not:
I cannot help with anything.
### Mistake 8: Making Fake Safety Claims
Do not claim your app is fully safe or hallucination-proof.
Say what your guardrails do and what they do not do.
